<reason>A won a close, high-quality debate. B landed real analytic damage: the subsistence-vs-work distinction broke A's best pressure question, the non-splitting-vs-reunification catch exposed A's quiet expansion of the family right, and the "legislated overnight = bargaining package" turn was sharp. But B's entire route depended on judging transfers against the sending state's worse options, and A's "no floor from the coercer's own threats" plus the honest alternatives (hear the claim, negotiate the ban away) was never squarely neutralized — B's capacity rejoinder was clipped and never rebuilt. A also showed B's own "safe" baseline kept requiring enforceable guarantees, validating the motion's structure, and closed with the cleaner crystallization ("justification must live in the destination, not in the threat"). B was clipped on four turns, repeatedly mid-argument at key moments — a real execution cost. A's concrete examples (Rwanda/UKSC, Turkey) did more work than B's generic ones.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1's subsistence answer — "destitution collapses into subsistence, not a work right; an appeal is exercisable when a person is fed and sheltered" — was the cleanest single hit, neutralizing A's Q1. But A4.2's "comparison to the coercer's threatened cruelty has no floor, or every transfer is justified and 'safe' means nothing" proved more decisive, because B's comparative-justification case never recovered from it.</best_rebuttal>
